title: Curate: practice edits and preserve their history
description: Practice reversible mask and track edits in the nested Curate tool, with explicitly synthetic data and external checkpoints for the current mask-history limitation.
objectives: Find Curate inside Make Masks and open unchanged copies of the teaching mask and tracks.
Paint, undo and save a mask without treating a practice mark as a biological correction.
Preserve saved masks and sidecars outside the application before reopening.
Split and join tracks, save their history and discard an unsaved deletion.
prerequisite: Extract Curate_SYNTHETIC_practice.zip and work on copies. The TIFF preserves label plane 2 of the recorded synthetic Timelapse output: 256 by 256 pixels, sixteen labels numbered 2 through 17. The CSV has sixteen tracks and 128 rows across eight frames. These are not acquired biological data. The current NPY picker path failed to load; this example uses exact integer TIFF labels. Brush radius 8, New label 18 and an empty-area click are practice settings, not biological corrections. Independent array checks verify every pixel after paint, undo, save and reload. Save mask writes the selected file and its .curation.json sidecar. The native mask reload loses its three-entry in-memory log, and the next save replaces the sidecar with one new entry. This defect remains unfixed. Before reopening, run the separate companion curate_checkpoint.py with the saved mask path and a NEW backup folder; it preserves both files byte-for-byte and refuses overwrite. Keep separate checkpoints and notes; it does not restore app history or merge ledgers. Reopening adds a second viewer mask layer, so changed colour intensity is not changed label identity. Track 2 split at frame 4 creates track 18; joining the non-overlapping halves restores all 128 rows. Joining tracks 2 and 3 is refused because frames overlap. A saved split/join log survives reloading after an unsaved deletion of track 3. All CSV values and original source hashes are checked. No accuracy claim, new segmentation, GPU, AI request, app modification or publication. API: spacr.curation.MaskCuration and TrackCuration; GUI persistence differs as disclosed.

scenes.narration: Open Make Masks, then its nested Curate tool. Curate belongs under Make Masks in the submodule section, not on a separate Home tile. It edits label masks and tracks. This lesson uses synthetic teaching outputs from Timelapse, not acquired biological observations or evidence that manual edits improve accuracy.

Download the linked practice archive and work on copies. Browse to its integer mask TIFF: sixteen original labels occupy this two hundred fifty-six pixel square. The picker also advertises NPY, but that route failed in this build. The TIFF preserves the exact label plane; do not replace labels with a coloured screenshot.

Set brush radius to eight and click New to select label eighteen. Paint once in the empty practice area. This disk is deliberately invented to learn the control; it is not a missing cell. The brush changes label pixels in memory, while the saved file remains unchanged until Save mask.

Undo stroke restores every original pixel in this exercise. Paint again, then inspect the result before saving. The recorded ledger contains paint, undo and paint; undo is itself part of the history. Your precise mouse position may change the painted pixel count, so do not treat our practice footprint as a biological target.

Save mask writes back to the selected working TIFF and saves its curation sidecar. Before reopening, run the separate checkpoint script supplied with the download, specifying this saved mask and a new backup folder. It copies both files exactly. This is an explicit external backup step, not a hidden application feature.

Here is the current limitation: reopening the mask resets its in-memory log, and another save replaces the sidecar with the new session's edit. Our earlier checkpoint still preserves the original three entries. Keep separate backups and notes; the script does not repair or restore app history. Reopening also adds a viewer layer, so colour brightness is not label identity.

Browse to the working tracks CSV. It has sixteen tracks over eight frames, with one hundred twenty-eight rows. Selecting tracks two and three and pressing Join is refused because both exist in the same frames. Read that message; forcing unrelated trajectories together would not be a valid correction.

Select track two, set Split at frame to four, and click Split. Frames four through seven move to new track eighteen, while frames zero through three remain in track two. Coordinates and original labels stay unchanged. This is a controlled editing exercise, not evidence of a real cell division.

Select tracks two and eighteen together and click Join. Their non-overlapping halves combine, restoring all original rows. Click Save tracks to write the CSV and its own sidecar. The independent check compares every frame, identifier and coordinate, not just the number of tracks. Keep the mask and track histories distinct.

Deleting track three removes its eight rows in memory. Do not save this demonstration deletion. Reopen the saved CSV to discard that unsaved change. This illustrates the difference between current edits and disk contents; deleting a trajectory in real data requires a documented reason, not simply an unwanted result.

All one hundred twenty-eight rows and the saved split-and-join history return. Unlike mask reopening in this build, track reopening retains that history in our test. Preserve original data, checkpoints and reasons for edits. Python provides MaskCuration and TrackCuration; this workflow needs neither a GPU nor an AI provider, and successful editing is not scientific validation.
